passage:
Day 1, Sunday. Himani tore open the bracelet-making kit and sang while sorting the coloured threads. Her father Nitin took a photo of her first bracelet, finished in an hour, bright pink and green.

Day 6, Friday. The second bracelet needed sixty tiny knots, one after another. Himani did twelve, sighed, and went to look at the fish tank instead.

Day 14, Saturday. Nitin found the kit under the bed, threads tangled. “Want to do one row a day?” he asked. Himani thought about it and said, “Maybe.” She tied one row that evening and then left, bored.

qa.q: How many knots did the second bracelet need?
qa.a: The second bracelet needed sixty tiny knots.

qa.q: Why did Himani go to look at the fish tank on Day 6?
qa.a: Himani was bored by the repeated knots, and the fish tank was more interesting; the excitement of starting had faded.

qa.q: What small step could help Himani finish the second bracelet?
qa.a: Tie a small number of knots each evening, perhaps with some music or a friend, and tick each row on a paper strip.

qa.q: How might Nitin feel finding the tangled kit under the bed?
qa.a: Nitin is probably a little disappointed but patient, since he asks about one row a day instead of scolding.

grounding: A child starts a craft kit with excitement and drops it when the novelty fades.

passage: “You want to stop the model ship already, Abhinav? Sit. I'm Harish, and I was ten when I got a shiny new diary with a lock, from my Bua in Nagpur. Page one, two, three, four: I wrote everything, even what I ate. On the fifth day I was tired and wrote nothing. On the sixth I said, tomorrow I'll write double. The diary went into a drawer, and the key into the drain, I think. Every January afterwards I bought a new one, and every February it was empty. Only when I was fifteen did I write a single boring line every night: just the date and one thing. Even a dull page counts, I found.”

qa.q: Who gave Harish the diary at the age of ten?
qa.a: Harish's Bua in Nagpur gave the diary.

qa.q: How did Harish feel about the diary by the sixth day?
qa.a: Harish was tired and losing interest, and the promise to write double tomorrow shows a wish to avoid the flat middle.

qa.q: What choice at fifteen made the difference in the story?
qa.a: At fifteen Harish decided to write only the date and one thing each night, so even a dull page counted.

qa.q: How might Abhinav feel hearing this after wanting to quit the model ship?
qa.a: Abhinav may feel understood and a bit caught out, since Harish's diary story matches Abhinav's own wish to stop.

grounding: A child begins a diary with enthusiasm and abandons it when the flat middle arrives.

passage:
Sarika: "Ammi, look! A bead-bracelet kit! I'm going to make one for everyone in the class."
Farida: "Everyone? That's thirty-two bracelets, beta."
Sarika: "Easy. I'll do five a day."
(Three days later.)
Farida: "How many now?"
Sarika: "Four."
Farida: "Four today?"
Sarika: "Four total. Threading is boring, Ammi. The beads keep rolling away."
Farida: "Remember how excited you were on Sunday?"
Sarika: "That was the fun part. Choosing colours."
Farida: "What if we make one bracelet each evening, together, while we listen to the radio?"
Sarika: "Only one?"
Farida: "Only one. And you pick the song."
Sarika: "...Okay. But I'm choosing the loud songs."

qa.q: How many bracelets did Sarika plan to make?
qa.a: Sarika planned to make thirty-two bracelets, one for everyone in the class.

qa.q: How did Sarika's feelings about the kit change after three days?
qa.a: She went from excited on Sunday to bored and fed up, because threading was dull and the beads kept rolling away.

qa.q: What small step did Farida suggest, and why might it help?
qa.a: Making one bracelet each evening together with the radio on makes the boring middle shorter and more fun.

qa.q: What is it like for Farida to see Sarika give up so fast?
qa.a: Farida seems patient and understanding, gently reminding Sarika of Sunday's excitement and offering company rather than a scolding.

grounding: A dialogue shows a child who starts a craft kit with great excitement and drops it when the dull middle arrives.

passage: I'm Minakshi, and in Class 5 I got a diary with a lock and a tiny golden key for my birthday. My friend Kashish got one too. The first night I wrote three whole pages: my cake, my new shoes, what Kashish said at lunch. The second night, two pages. By the second week, I wrote "nothing happened today" and closed it. By the third week, it was under my bed with the key lost. It wasn't that I didn't like it. The first page felt like a party. The middle pages felt like homework. Kashish kept hers for a year. I still don't know how.

qa.q: What was special about Minakshi's birthday diary?
qa.a: It had a lock and a tiny golden key.

qa.q: How did Minakshi feel about the diary once the novelty wore off?
qa.a: Minakshi felt bored, as the middle pages felt like homework instead of a party.

qa.q: What could have helped Minakshi keep writing?
qa.a: Writing just one line a night or sharing entries with Kashish could make the flat middle less of a chore.

qa.q: How might Kashish see Minakshi's diary under the bed?
qa.a: Kashish might be surprised or a bit sad, since keeping the diary for a year came naturally to her.

grounding: A child looks back on starting a diary with great excitement and abandoning it once the novelty faded.

passage:
Note from the after-school art club coordinator, Thursday.
Aditi, age nine, started our weaving project on Monday with huge energy. She chose five colours of wool, drew a pattern and wove the first ten rows before anyone else had finished three. Today she stopped at row fourteen and asked to switch to clay. When I asked why, she said, "The middle is all the same colour. It's boring." I did not force her. I paired her with Preeti, who is steady at weaving, and we agreed Aditi would do two rows each session, then clay. She finished row sixteen today and went off happily.

qa.q: How many rows had Aditi woven by the time she asked to switch?
qa.a: She stopped at row fourteen.

qa.q: Why did Aditi want to switch to clay?
qa.a: She felt bored because the middle of the weaving was all the same colour, and the excitement of choosing colours had faded.

qa.q: How did the coordinator support Aditi, and what worked?
qa.a: The coordinator paired her with Preeti and set a small goal of two rows per session before clay, so the dull stretch felt manageable.

qa.q: How might Preeti be affected by being paired with Aditi?
qa.a: Preeti might feel proud to be trusted as the steady one, and gets a partner to chat with while weaving.

grounding: An adult's note shows a child beginning a craft with great excitement and wanting to drop it at the dull middle.

passage:
Dear Diary,
On Sunday I started a plant diary. Jyoti didi gave me a packet of bean seeds and a cup. I drew the cup with a ruler. I wrote "Day 1" in green pen with stars. I was SO excited.
Day 2, I drew the cup again. Nothing had happened. Day 3, same. Day 4 I forgot.
Today is Day 9. There is a tiny green hook coming out of the soil! But my diary has only three pages, and Days 4 to 8 are empty.
Jyoti didi said, "The boring days are part of the story too." I don't think boring days are a story. But I drew the green hook very carefully.
Maybe tomorrow I'll just write one line.
Harsha

qa.q: What did Jyoti didi give Harsha?
qa.a: A packet of bean seeds and a cup.

qa.q: How did Harsha feel on Day 1 compared with Days 2 and 3?
qa.a: Harsha felt very excited on Day 1, but on Days 2 and 3 the diary felt boring because nothing had happened.

qa.q: What small plan might help Harsha keep going through the flat middle?
qa.a: Writing just one line each day, even when nothing changes, as Harsha decides for tomorrow.

qa.q: How might Jyoti didi feel seeing the empty pages?
qa.a: Jyoti didi might feel a bit amused and understanding, and gently encourage Harsha to keep going.

grounding: Illustrates a child who starts a plant diary with great excitement and drops it when nothing seems to happen in the middle.
